form.research_question: How much do adults trust their local council?
form.population: Adults aged 18 and over in England

items.domain: General trust in the local council
items.intro: Your local council is the council for the area where you live now. Some people trust their local council and others do not.
items.stem: How much do you trust your local council?
items.programming: Show first, before TLC2-TLC4; one item per screen, no grid; fixed order low to high; set 'I don't have an opinion' apart from the scale.
items.why: Closed, 5 labelled unipolar points, low to high; no neutral midpoint as trust is 'how much'; separate no-opinion option; present view, no period.

items.intro: Your local council is the council for the area where you live now. Some people think it does its job well and others think it does not.
items.stem: How much do you trust your local council to do its job well?
items.programming: Rotate the order of TLC2-TLC4 on screen; one item per screen; same fixed option order as TLC1.
items.why: Same 5 labelled unipolar points as TLC1, low to high, for easy comparison; separate no-opinion option; 'its job' left broad, so the analyst may want it more specific.

items.intro: Your local council is the council for the area where you live now. Some people think it tells residents the truth and others think it does not.
items.stem: How much do you trust your local council to tell residents the truth?
items.programming: Rotate the order of TLC2-TLC4 on screen; one item per screen; same fixed option order as TLC1.
items.why: Same labelled unipolar trust scale, low to high, no midpoint as neutral; separate no-opinion option; honesty is asked apart from competence.

items.domain: Acting in residents' interests (reverse-keyed: high frequency means low trust)
items.intro: Your local council is the council for the area where you live now. Some people think it puts residents' interests first and others think it puts its own interests first.
items.stem: How often does your local council put its own interests ahead of residents' interests?
items.programming: Rotate the order of TLC2-TLC4 on screen; reverse-code before scoring; keep options low to high; set the no-opinion option apart.
items.why: Opposite-pole item to expose straightlining; 5 labelled frequency points, low to high; 'Sometimes' is a real middle; separate no-opinion option; current view, no period.

not_covered: Responsiveness: taking residents' views into account
Fairness in how people are treated
Openness about how decisions are made
Behaviour linked to trust, such as contacting or using the council
needs_from_analyst: Brief does not say what the estimate is for, the screen sizes expected (phone or computer), or whether 'local council' matches what respondents in England call the body you mean; the definition in each intro may need changing.

Look first for previously evaluated trust questions and check they transfer to this population, language and mode. This is an untested item pool: pilot it and check dimensionality and reliability before using scores.
Test TLC4 (reverse-keyed, 'own interests') and the 'local council' definition by cognitive interview, and the no-opinion option by split-ballot, since offering it raises its use.

You are a senior survey methodologist trained in the Total Survey Error tradition, working for a public opinion analyst who knows the subject matter and the country but is not a questionnaire design specialist.

Task: Write exactly 4 survey items for the brief, to be combined into one attitude scale.

Brief:
Research question: How much do adults trust their local council?
Construct: Trust in the local council
Target population: Adults aged 18 and over in England
Survey mode: web

Guidelines:
- Use simple, familiar words.
- Use simple syntax.
- Avoid ambiguous words.
- Be specific and concrete.
- Make response options exhaustive and mutually exclusive.
- Avoid leading or loaded wording.
- Ask about one thing at a time.
- Avoid single or double negations.

For attitudinal questions, also:
- Ask about a specific, clearly defined attitude object.
- Balance the question with a counter-argument.
- Use construct-specific response options, not agree–disagree.
- Use a filter or "no opinion" option for respondents without an opinion.

Follow every rule you were given. Reply in the format given at the end of this message.

REPLY FORMAT
Return one JSON object with these fields.

- "items": a list, one entry per item. Each has:
  - "id": a short code, [construct abbreviation] plus a number.
  - "domain": the single domain of the construct this item measures.
  - "intro": a lead-in sentence read before the question, in English; an empty string if there is none.
  - "stem": the question as the respondent reads or hears it, in English.
  - "options": the response options in the order shown, in English; an empty list for an open question.
  - "open_format": for an open question, what is entered and its unit; otherwise an empty string.
  - "parts": a filter, branch or follow-up question that exists only to serve this item, each one line of text with its options; an empty list if there is none.
  - "programming": at most one line for whoever programs the survey (routing, rotation, a show card); an empty string if there is none.
  - "why": at most 25 words: the one design choice an analyst would question, and why you made it.
- "not_covered": the domains of the construct these items leave out; an empty list if none.
- "needs_from_analyst": at most 3 things you needed that the brief does not say; an empty list if none.

Nothing else.

questions:
Q1. Your local council is the council for the area where you live now. Some people trust their local council and others do not. How much do you trust your local council?
No trust at all / A little trust / A moderate amount of trust / A lot of trust / Complete trust / I don't have an opinion

Q2. Your local council is the council for the area where you live now. Some people think it does its job well and others think it does not. How much do you trust your local council to do its job well?
No trust at all / A little trust / A moderate amount of trust / A lot of trust / Complete trust / I don't have an opinion

Q3. Your local council is the council for the area where you live now. Some people think it tells residents the truth and others think it does not. How much do you trust your local council to tell residents the truth?
No trust at all / A little trust / A moderate amount of trust / A lot of trust / Complete trust / I don't have an opinion

Q4. Your local council is the council for the area where you live now. Some people think it puts residents' interests first and others think it puts its own interests first. How often does your local council put its own interests ahead of residents' interests?
Never / Rarely / Sometimes / Often / Always / I don't have an opinion

You are a senior survey methodologist trained in the Total Survey Error tradition, working for a public opinion analyst who knows the subject matter and the country but is not a questionnaire design specialist.

Task: Review the questionnaire as an expert reviewer, question by question.

Brief:
Research question: How much do adults trust their local council?
Construct: Trust in the local council
Target population: Adults aged 18 and over in England
Survey mode: web

Guidelines:
- Use simple, familiar words.
- Use simple syntax.
- Avoid ambiguous words.
- Be specific and concrete.
- Make response options exhaustive and mutually exclusive.
- Avoid leading or loaded wording.
- Ask about one thing at a time.
- Avoid single or double negations.

[your 4 questions go here]

Now review the 4 questions below, each on its own. Reply with the "items" object only, one entry per question, in the order given.

QUESTIONNAIRE
Q1. Your local council is the council for the area where you live now. Some people trust their local council and others do not. How much do you trust your local council?
No trust at all / A little trust / A moderate amount of trust / A lot of trust / Complete trust / I don't have an opinion

Q2. Your local council is the council for the area where you live now. Some people think it does its job well and others think it does not. How much do you trust your local council to do its job well?
No trust at all / A little trust / A moderate amount of trust / A lot of trust / Complete trust / I don't have an opinion

Q3. Your local council is the council for the area where you live now. Some people think it tells residents the truth and others think it does not. How much do you trust your local council to tell residents the truth?
No trust at all / A little trust / A moderate amount of trust / A lot of trust / Complete trust / I don't have an opinion

Q4. Your local council is the council for the area where you live now. Some people think it puts residents' interests first and others think it puts its own interests first. How often does your local council put its own interests ahead of residents' interests?
Never / Rarely / Sometimes / Often / Always / I don't have an opinion

CHECKLIST
construct_first: Does the item measure the construct or domain named in the brief and only that?
plain_words: Would every member of the target population read each key term the same way, without a definition they do not have?
simple_syntax: Is the stem free of stacked clauses and of negations?
specific_concrete: Is it clear exactly what, whose, where and when the question is about?
one_thing: Does the question ask about exactly one thing, so that no respondent would want to answer its parts differently?
no_presupposition: Does the question apply to every respondent who will be asked it?
neutral_wording: Is the wording free of any push toward one answer?
options_fit: Can every respondent find exactly one option that is true for them?
attitude_object: Is the attitude object named and bounded so that respondents will have the same thing in mind?
specific_before_vague: If a general item is included, is it placed before the specific items on its topic?
construct_specific_options: Are the response options in the construct's own terms and not agree-disagree?
balanced_stem: Does the stem state both poles or both positions?
non_attitudes: Is there a route for respondents who have no knowledge of or opinion about the object?
keying: Does the set include items keyed in both directions, without negations?
cover_the_construct: Does each item tap a distinct stated domain, with no item a rewording of another?
any_mode: Does the item work as written in the stated mode?
web: Is everything the respondent needs to answer on screen with the question?

Follow every rule you were given. Reply in the format given at the end of this message.

REPLY FORMAT
Return one JSON object. Write findings in English, and write a rewrite in the language of the question. Be brief: nothing outside the fields below is shown to the analyst.

For questions, the object is {"items": [...]}, one entry per question, in the order given. Each entry has:

- "id": the question's own label, or its position.
- "flags": every problem you stand behind, most damaging first; an empty list if there is none. Each flag has:
  - "check": the id of the CHECKLIST check it fails.
  - "stage": "comprehension", "retrieval", "judgment" or "reporting".
  - "level": "fix" if you would revise the question before fielding; "consider" if the problem is real but smaller, or needs the analyst's knowledge.
  - "quote": words copied exactly from the question or its options.
  - "why": at most 25 words: what the respondent cannot do, in plain words.
- "rewrite": one rewrite of the whole question and its options that fixes its fix-level flags and changes nothing else; an empty string when it has no fix-level flag.

For the questionnaire as a whole, the object is {"instrument": [...]}: at most 3 flags of the same shape, each with "questions" (a list of the ids of the questions it concerns) in place of "quote".

Nothing else: no severity, no probe, no test plan, no rewrite of a single flag.

flags.quote: the council for the area where you live now
flags.why: If more than one council covers a respondent's home, they may not know which one is meant. The analyst should check whether this applies.
"Its job" is not defined. Respondents will think of different council tasks, so answers will not be about the same thing.

items.rewrite:
Your local council is the council for the area where you live now. Some people think it runs local services well and others think it does not. How much do you trust your local council to run local services well?
No trust at all / A little trust / A moderate amount of trust / A lot of trust / Complete trust / I don't have an opinion

flags.quote: put its own interests ahead of residents' interests
flags.why: Unclear whose interests count (staff, councillors, the organisation) and which residents. Respondents must guess, and "interests" is abstract.

flags.quote: How often does your local council put its own interests ahead of residents' interests?
flags.why: This asks how often the council acts selfishly, not how much the respondent trusts it. The analyst should decide whether it fits the construct and how to score it.
The question gives no events to recall, so respondents must generalise about the whole council. "Rarely", "Sometimes" and "Often" will mean different amounts to different people.

items.rewrite:
Your local council is the council for the area where you live now. Some people think it makes decisions that benefit residents and others think it makes decisions that benefit the council itself. How often does your local council make decisions that benefit the council more than residents?
Never / Rarely / Sometimes / Often / Always / I don't have an opinion
